{"name":"6fe73b51f9e0e6c0f86a","layouts":[{"id":0,"position":{"x":10,"y":91,"z":2000,"width":1260,"height":909,"tabOrder":2000}}],"singleVisual":{"visualType":"textbox","drillFilterOtherVisuals":true,"objects":{"general":[{"properties":{"paragraphs":[{"textRuns":[{"value":"In the frailty CPG report all data shown related to those who are aged 65 or over or those who were aged 65 and over at the time of their activity and with a frailty category of Mild, Moderate or Severe frailty at the time of their activity. e.g. on the ED attendances tab data is shown for patients age 65+ with a frailty score of mild frailty or above at the time of attendance. "}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"How is frailty determined","textStyle":{"fontWeight":"bold"}}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Frailty can be established by using two different types of score (1) electronic frailty index (eFI) or (2) Rockwood score.","textStyle":{"fontSize":"10pt"}}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":" "}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"eFI uses a cumulative deficit model to identify and score frailty based on the number of deficits presented by the patient within the primary care data through read codes. The eFI uses a subset of these read codes to interpret any number of up to 36 potential deficits. The number of deficits that an individual is considered to have is then divided by the total (36) to produce a score. This score determines whether a person is considered fit, mildly frail, moderately frail, or severely frail and nearing the end of their life. The frailty categories are determined as follows:","textStyle":{"fontSize":"10pt"}}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":" -  "},{"value":"Fit","textStyle":{"textDecoration":"underline"}},{"value":": up to 4 deficits"}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":" -  "},{"value":"Mild Frailty","textStyle":{"textDecoration":"underline"}},{"value":": 5 to 8 deficits"}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":" -  "},{"value":"Moderate Frailty","textStyle":{"textDecoration":"underline"}},{"value":": 9 to 12 deficits"}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":" -  "},{"value":"Severe Frailty","textStyle":{"textDecoration":"underline"}},{"value":": 13 deficits and above "}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"The eFI is based upon a person’s needs, rather than their service use and so it can be used to identify people with lower levels of frailty before they have significant unplanned service use. Therefore these individuals can be targeted with appropriate preventative interventions.","textStyle":{"fontSize":"10pt"}}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"All patients within Gloucester have a recorded eFI and two patients can have the same frailty score but a completely different mix of deficits.","textStyle":{"fontSize":"10pt"}}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":" "}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Rockwood scores utilise a sarcopenia model of frailty rather than a cumulative model. Patients only get a Rockwood upon evaluation by clinician. The score can be between 1 and 9; 1 = 1 fit, 8 = very severely frail and 9 = 9 terminally ill. Rockwood is only recorded if clinician is concerned about the patient. It can also be done in ED but this is often in a crisis state so is often not reflective of the patients overall status. ","textStyle":{"fontSize":"10pt"}}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Therefore, use of a Rockwood score is good for individual level frailty at a specified time while eFI is more reflective of day to da","textStyle":{"fontSize":"10pt"}},{"value":"y condition and is better for viewing frailty from a higher population level."}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"This report uses eFI as its is better record across our entire population and allows the analysis of high level trends. "}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Rate per 1000","textStyle":{"fontWeight":"bold","textDecoration":"underline"}}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"The majority of the data is shown as a rate per 1000 to account for the population variation across frailty categories as well as localities, PCNs, deprivation cohorts, age cohorts etc. ","textStyle":{"fontSize":"10pt"}}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"A \"rate per 1,000\" is a method of expressing a specific number of occurrences or events relative to a population size of 1,000 individuals. It is used to standardise and compare frequencies of events across different populations or groups. This measure allows for easier comparison between groups of different sizes by normalising the data. Rates per 1,000 are commonly used in public health, demography, and other fields to report and compare data like birth rates, mortality rates, incidence rates of diseases, and other demographic or health-related events."}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Any chart that shows rate per 1000 over time will  be using the population at the time of the activity to calculate the rate i.e. the rate per 1000 in April 2019 is calculated based on the frail category populations in April 2019 where in April 2022 the rate per 1000 is calculated based on the frail category populations in April 2022. "}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"However in any chart where a time series is not shown only shows activity from 2023/24 and is calculating rate per 1000 based on the current frail category populations. "}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Deprivation Deciles","textStyle":{"fontWeight":"bold","textDecoration":"underline"}}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Deprivation deciles are based on the Index of Multiple Deprivation 2019 (IMD 2019). Decile 1 represents the most deprived 10% (or decile) of small areas in England, and Decile 10 represents the least deprived 10%."}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"In order to compare metrics locally, Gloucestershire deprivation deciles are sometimes used (also used in this report). This is created in the same way as the national deciles, though Decile 1 reflects the most deprived 10% within the county rather than nationally, and Decile 10 represents the least deprived 10% within the county."}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Ethnicity Hierarchy","textStyle":{"fontWeight":"bold","textDecoration":"underline"}}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Ethnicity data can be sparsely collected in some service areas, therefore an ethnicity hierarchy has been created to ensure we have the best quality ethnicity data recorded for each patient. The hierarchy searches for valid ethnicity records from the below service areas. We assume records collected at the top of the hierarchy will be more reliable than those at the bottom of the hierarchy and therefore we will prioritise records from those areas first."}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Primary care Data"}],"listType":"ordered"},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Adult Social Care"}],"listType":"ordered"},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Outpatient Data"}],"listType":"ordered"},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Community Data"}],"listType":"ordered"},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Mental Health Data"}],"listType":"ordered"},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Inpatient Data"}],"listType":"ordered"},{"textRuns":[{"value":"Accident and Emergency Data"}],"listType":"ordered"},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]},{"textRuns":[{"value":""}]}]}}]},"vcObjects":{"title":[{"properties":{"titleWrap":{"expr":{"Literal":{"Value":"true"}}}}}],"background":[{"properties":{"show":{"expr":{"Literal":{"Value":"true"}}},"transparency":{"expr":{"Literal":{"Value":"0D"}}}}}],"general":[{"properties":{"keepLayerOrder":{"expr":{"Literal":{"Value":"true"}}}}}],"visualHeader":[{"properties":{"show":{"expr":{"Literal":{"Value":"false"}}}}}]}}}
